title: POC weekly sync - SDK tool/function calls & structured output
summary: Weekly POC sync covering SDK function/tool-calling integration, structured output schema discussion, early benchmark results, and next steps for validation and security review. Customer requested clearer examples for nested tool calls and guidance on handling schema validation errors and kerneling caching concerns.
next_steps: SE to share updated SDK example repo for nested tool/function calls (link)
Customer to run integration benchmark with the provided example and post results in shared spreadsheet
Schedule security follow-up with Quanta infra team to review SSO/KMS details (tentative next week)
AE to send commercial pilot template and rough pricing estimate

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-15
Time: 10:00 AM PST
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Quanta CTO), Maya Lopez (Quanta Lead ML Eng), Jordan Blake (Quanta PM)
--
[00:00] Alex Chen: okay good morning everyone, thanks for joining. we wanted to run through the SDK integration updates and the function/tool calling stuff you were testing last week. Priya will lead the technical bits.
[00:18] Priya Nair: hey all. quick agenda: one, review the integration results Maya shared; two, show an updated SDK snippet for nested tool calls and structured output; three, talk about error handling and validation; four, next steps. sound good?
[00:32] Maya Lopez: yup that works. quick note, the benchmark spreadsheet is here - i put the run with 1k samples in the sheet, link in the chat. some of the responses are missing fields when using the structured schema so want to dig into why.
[00:48] Priya Nair: got it, we expected a couple edge cases. two likely causes: prompt/template mismatch with schema enforcement, or race on asynchronous tool calls when you chain functions.
[01:05] Samir Patel: can you clarify "tool calls" in the SDK? is that the function-calling feature you showed in the demo where the model suggests a call to an internal API?
[01:14] Priya Nair: yeah that's right. in the SDK we have two common patterns: lightweight tool invocation where the model returns a structured function call payload and the app executes it, and server-side execution where Redwood can proxy or run managed tool hooks. for the POC you're doing the client-side execution pattern.
[01:32] Jordan Blake: one thing we saw — when the model returns a function call and we call our downstream patient-data service, sometimes the function args are flattened incorrectly, or nested objects get stringified. any best practices?
[01:44] Priya Nair: yep, that's usually due to JSON serialization differences. in the SDK snippet i shared today, we show explicit typing for function arguments and a small validation step: parse the function call payload, run it against the JSON schema (we include ajv example), and then call the downstream service. if validation fails, fallback to a clarification turn to the model rather than calling your service.
[02:10] Maya Lopez: we tried ajv but some validation errors are cryptic; would be helpful if Redwood's SDK could return a human-readable reason why the field failed.
[02:20] Priya Nair: that's fair. we can add helper utils in the example wrapper that map ajv errors into readable hints. action item on our side.
[02:30] Alex Chen: quick commercial note — Samir, you mentioned wanting predictable latency for live patient workflows. we should keep an eye on dedicated vs hosted here.
[02:42] Samir Patel: yes, latency SLOs are important; also we have compliance constraints so we may need VPC or private. how does that affect the function-calling architecture?
[02:53] Priya Nair: if you're on Private or Dedicated, the runtime can live in your VPC and the SDK usage is the same. function calls that hit internal APIs can remain within the network. only difference is we recommend pinning model versions and enabling KV/prefix caching carefully so that you control any data residency.
[03:12] Jordan Blake: about caching — is there a risk that KV cache returns stale context for patient notes if the downstream DB updates right after a call?
[03:21] Priya Nair: caching is workload-specific. for sensitive, high-churn data we recommend short TTLs or bypass caching for those routes. Redwood Optimize can help recommend per-route caching policies based on requests/sec and staleness tolerance.
[03:35] Maya Lopez: back to the missing fields — the spreadsheet shows about 7% of responses missing "diagnosis.code" field in the structured output. the prompt we used includes the schema, but sometimes model paraphrases.
[03:47] Priya Nair: two suggestions: 1) prefer function-calling mode where you declare the function signature with typed params — model will output the exact args; 2) add a post-generation validation/repair step: if a field missing, call a short "fill-missing-fields" prompt that instructs model to return only the JSON with missing keys filled. we've included that pattern in the SDK example.
[04:12] Samir Patel: how about cost impact of doing a second turn to repair? that doubles token use for the examples where it happens.
[04:20] Priya Nair: correct, there's cost tradeoff. you can mitigate by: only doing repair when validation fails (so sparse), or run a lightweight deterministic rule-based filler for trivial defaults. also, batching and prefix caching can reduce overall token spend.
[04:38] Jordan Blake: any numbers from your internal benchmarks? we need rough cost delta per 1k requests for using repair step vs not.
[04:46] Priya Nair: we have a sample in the shared sheet: repair added roughly 12-18% token overhead on our test set depending on how verbose the model was. i'll paste that specific row.
[04:57] Maya Lopez: ok thanks. another integration issue — when chaining two function calls (e.g., call A returns id used by call B), we saw race conditions if calls are parallelized. is there a recommended orchestration pattern?
[05:10] Priya Nair: for sequential dependencies, do them synchronously client-side: wait for validated output from call A before invoking call B. if you need throughput, use optimistic parallelization with compensating actions on failure, but that's more architecture work. the SDK shows a small helper 'chainFunctionsSequentially' to simplify this.
[05:30] Alex Chen: can you show the snippet now, Priya? maybe screen-share?
[05:36] Priya Nair: i'm going to paste the main snippet in chat; apologies if formatting is off. (shared code)
[05:45] Priya Nair: // SDK example (pseudo)
const response = await redwood.sdk.callModel({
  model: 'redwood-2b',
  functions: [ { name: 'createPatientNote', paramsSchema: patientNoteSchema }, { name: 'flagForReview', paramsSchema: flagSchema } ],
  // use function_call: 'auto' or explicit name to force
});
const fn = response.function_call;
try {
  const args = JSON.parse(fn.arguments);
  validateAgainstSchema(args, fn.paramsSchema);
  await callDownstreamService(fn.name, args);
} catch (e) {
  // validation failed - request repair turn from model
  const repair = await redwood.sdk.generate({ prompt: repairPromptFor(fn.paramsSchema, fn.arguments) });
  // parse and re-run validation...
}
[06:35] Maya Lopez: that looks close to what we built. couple notes: our downstream requires dates in ISO and sometimes model returns natural language dates.
[06:44] Priya Nair: yep we've seen that; include a small adapter layer that normalizes common types (dates, enums). we also recommend unit tests that assert schema conformance for each function call payload.
[06:58] Samir Patel: on security — we need to know what logs Redwood retains. audit logs, full request/response retention?
[07:06] Alex Chen: good question. by default hosted has short retention; in Dedicated/Private you control logs. we can share a SOC2 security pack and the retention options; i'll attach the security doc after this call.
[07:18] Maya Lopez: please do. also need to confirm KMS integration for encrypting model cache and any persisted data.
[07:25] Priya Nair: Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSMs, and there is an integration guide. we'll put the KMS section in the follow-up security email.
[07:35] Jordan Blake: switching to observability — when a function call fails, what's the best way to trace and debug? do you surface the model function call id in logs?
[07:44] Priya Nair: yes each call has a tokenized call id. Redwood Console shows per-call latencies, per-function error rates, and you can click into the request to see the payload (if you have retention enabled). for PII routes we recommend redacting payloads but keeping metadata and hashed IDs.
[08:02] Maya Lopez: great. our infra team will want a demo of the console traces. can we set that up after security signoff?
[08:10] Alex Chen: yes we can schedule that with a console demo and some sample traces.
[08:15] Samir Patel: question on model variants — are you suggesting quantized models for cost savings? how does that affect structured output fidelity?
[08:25] Priya Nair: quantized models can be fine for many structured output tasks, but we empirically test each model/quantization profile with your prompts. Redwood Optimize will recommend profiles; for strict schema fidelity we often recommend using a slightly larger fp16 model or a verified quantization profile.
[08:42] Jordan Blake: is there an automated regression alert if structured output fidelity drops between model versions?
[08:48] Priya Nair: yes, Redwood has eval hooks to run your prompt set on a candidate model and fail rollouts if key metrics (like field completion or hallucination rate) degrade. we can wire up your QA prompt set into that pipeline.
[09:02] Maya Lopez: that's important. we'll export our 200 test prompts and share.
[09:08] Alex Chen: noted. next, any blockers from your side for the pilot?
[09:14] Maya Lopez: main blockers: 1) clearer SDK examples for nested tool calls and repair flows; 2) security/KMS confirmation; 3) end-to-end benchmark with real latency numbers from our network.
[09:25] Priya Nair: we'll cover 1 today and share code. for 3, we need you to run the benchmark with the SDK snippet in your environment; we'll provide a runner script.
[09:37] Jordan Blake: about the runner script — can it do warmup, and do you recommend a fixed prompt set or randomized?
[09:44] Priya Nair: warmup is important to get realistic latencies for JIT and cache priming. we recommend using your production-ish prompt set (a mix) but include a warmup of ~200 requests. the runner will support both fixed and randomized modes.
[09:58] Samir Patel: timeline question — if we finish benchmarks and are happy, how quickly can we spin up Dedicated? 3-4 weeks?
[10:06] Alex Chen: typical lead for Dedicated GPU capacity provisioning is 2-6 weeks depending on config and contract. we can prioritize but need a signed pilot commitment.
[10:15] Samir Patel: understood. we'll align internally.
[10:20] Maya Lopez: small nit — in the SDK example the function schema name references 'patientNoteSchema' but we couldn't find that file in the repo link.
[10:29] Priya Nair: thanks, that was a packaging miss. i'll push a patch to the example repo and send the link.
[10:36] Jordan Blake: can you also include an end-to-end test that verifies the chain A->B sequence? that would catch the race condition.
[10:44] Priya Nair: yes we'll add a sample e2e test and a CI job to run it.
[10:50] Alex Chen: getting near the end of time — let's do a quick recap and owners.
[10:55] Priya Nair: recap: 1) Priya will share updated SDK examples with helper utils (validation mapping, date normalizers, chain helper) and add e2e tests; 2) Maya to run the benchmark with the runner script and upload results; 3) Alex to send security docs + pilot commercial template; 4) schedule infra security call next week.
[11:16] Maya Lopez: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[11:20] Samir Patel: thanks, appreciate it.
[11:25] Alex Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up with links and a calendar invite for the security deep dive. bye.
--
